title: Emotions and Relationships
description: Ten essays, columns and stories about the feelings that connect people: gratitude, apologies, nostalgia, a friendship across generations, envy, a long marriage, homesickness, forgiveness, neighbors and a father and son.

lessons.title: The Science of Gratitude
lessons.summary: An essay on how psychologists have studied gratitude, what they found and what they warn against.
lessons.text:
For most of history, gratitude belonged to priests, poets and grandmothers. It was a virtue to be praised, not measured. In recent decades, however, psychologists have tried to put it on an empirical footing, which means testing claims about it with observation and data rather than with sermons.

The first problem was a conceptual one: what exactly is being measured? Is gratitude an emotion that comes and goes, like surprise, or a lasting trait, like patience? Researchers settled on a careful formulation: gratitude is the recognition that something good has happened to us and that its source lies, at least partly, outside ourselves. The formulation sounds dry, but it does useful conceptual work: it separates gratitude from simple happiness, because you can be happy about good weather without feeling grateful to anyone.

The best-known empirical studies are simple. In one classic design, volunteers are divided into three groups. One group writes down, once a week, five things they are grateful for; another lists five daily troubles; a third records ordinary events. After ten weeks, the grateful group tends to report more optimism and slightly better sleep. In some studies, a subset of the grateful group, mostly those who wrote the most specific lists, also reported fewer headaches. That subset is small, however.

Other studies use hypothetical situations. They ask people to imagine that a stranger has helped them carry a heavy suitcase up a flight of stairs, and then they offer a hypothetical choice: would you rather keep ten dollars or give some of it to another stranger? People who have just recalled a moment of gratitude tend to share more. Gratitude, it seems, turns into generosity, and generosity, received by someone else, can produce gratitude in return.

More recently, scientists have built computational models of this cycle. A computational model is a set of rules run on a computer, in which thousands of imaginary people meet, help or ignore one another. In many such models, a little gratitude keeps generosity alive in a group for much longer, because people who are thanked are more likely to help again.

Some books and websites tout gratitude as a cure for almost everything, from loneliness to high blood pressure, and they tout special journals and apps to go with it. Here scientists tend to be cautious. A few studies have looked for metabolic effects, such as changes in blood sugar or in the way the body uses energy, but the metabolic evidence is weak so far. Researchers reiterate, in paper after paper, that gratitude is not a medicine.

What they reiterate just as often is more modest and more encouraging. Gratitude costs nothing, it can be practiced, and it tends to make people kinder to each other. That is not a miracle, but it is a good deal.

Questions:
What does an empirical approach to gratitude mean?
It means testing claims about gratitude with observation and data rather than with sermons.
How does the researchers' formulation separate gratitude from simple happiness?
In their formulation, gratitude means that the source of something good lies partly outside ourselves.
Who tends to share more in the hypothetical choice about ten dollars?
People who have just recalled a moment of gratitude tend to share more.
What do the computational models suggest?
They suggest that a little gratitude keeps generosity alive in a group for much longer.
What do researchers reiterate about gratitude?
They reiterate that it is not a medicine, but that it can make people kinder.

lessons.title: Why Apologies Work or Fail
lessons.summary: A parent looks at a child's apology note and at what research and the courts say about apologies.
lessons.text:
On the door of our refrigerator there is a note my daughter wrote when she was seven. It says: "I am sory [sic] I broke your cup. It was an acident [sic]. I will be more carful [sic]." The spelling is faulty, but as an apology it is almost perfect. It names what happened, it admits responsibility, and it promises to do better. Many adults with far better spelling do worse.

Researchers who study apologies tend to list the same parts. A good apology says what went wrong, accepts the blame, recognizes the harm done to the other person and offers some repair. When one of these parts is missing, the apology begins to feel faulty, like a machine with a loose screw.

The most common failure is the apology that tries to divert attention. "I'm sorry if you were upset" diverts attention from what the speaker did to how the listener feels, as if the problem were the listener's sensitivity. Another failure is the word "but." "I'm sorry, but you started it" is not an apology; that little "but" is enough to disqualify it. Even a beautiful apology can disqualify itself with one excuse. A third failure is the apology that turns into an interrogation: "I said I'm sorry. What else do you want? Why are you still angry?" An apology that becomes an interrogation of the injured person tends to alienate them further, and an alienated friend is harder to win back than an angry one.

Courts offer another view. Jurors are asked to decide whether someone broke the law, but they also form an opinion of that person's character. Studies suggest that jurors often respond well to a sincere apology and badly to one that sounds prepared by a lawyer. A juror, after all, is an ordinary person, and ordinary people hear the difference. For a long time, lawyers warned their clients never to apologize, because an apology might be treated as a confession. Some states have since passed laws that make it lawful for a doctor to express sympathy to a patient without that sympathy being used against the doctor in court. A lawful "I am so sorry this happened" can calm a family that might otherwise sue.

Should you prepare an apology beforehand? It helps to think beforehand about what you did and why it hurt. It does not help to practice a speech so polished that it sounds like an announcement from a company. People also tend to censor themselves at the crucial moment, removing the one sentence that matters most, such as "I was wrong." If you censor that sentence, the rest rarely works.

My daughter is now twelve, and her spelling has improved. Her apologies, I am pleased to say, have stayed simple. The note stays on the refrigerator as a reminder to the rest of us.

Questions:
Why is the daughter's note almost a perfect apology?
It names what happened, admits responsibility and promises to do better, although its spelling is faulty.
How does "I'm sorry if you were upset" divert attention?
It diverts attention from what the speaker did to how the listener feels.
What happens when an apology becomes an interrogation?
It tends to alienate the injured person further.
How do jurors often respond to apologies?
They respond well to a sincere apology and badly to one that sounds prepared by a lawyer.
What should you do beforehand?
You should think about what you did and why it hurt.

lessons.title: In Praise of Nostalgia
lessons.summary: A woman bakes her grandmother's bread and reflects on why nostalgia can be a useful feeling.
lessons.text:
For a long time, nostalgia had a bad reputation. The word was invented in 1688 by a Swiss medical student, who used it to describe a sickness he had seen in soldiers far from home. For two centuries, doctors treated nostalgia as a disorder, and later critics treated it as a weakness: a taste for yesterday's newspapers and a refusal to live in the present. Psychologists today take a kinder view. Their studies suggest that nostalgia, in moderate amounts, can lift our mood, make us feel less alone and remind us that our lives have meaning.

I thought about this last winter, when I baked my grandmother's rye bread for the first time. She baked a loaf every Saturday for fifty years, in a kitchen that always smelled smoky, because the old wood stove leaked when the wind blew from the north. Her recipe was written on a card in pencil, and half the instructions were missing. "Add flour until it feels right," it said. The loaf that came out of my oven was flatter than hers, but the smell was exactly the same, and for a moment I was nine years old again.

While the bread cooled, I took down the box of things my mother had given me after my grandmother died. Inside was a small wooden carving of a bird, which my grandfather had made with a small knife. The carving is rough, and one wing is shorter than the other, but you can see that he took his time. There was also a ticket from the world exposition in Seattle in 1962, which my grandparents visited on their honeymoon. They talked about that exposition for the rest of their lives, as if they had traveled to the future and come back. Between the pages of an old cookbook, I found a pressed rose. Each petal had turned the color of tea, and when I touched one petal, it broke into dust.

What struck me was how ordinary these objects were, and how much they held. Researchers have found that the memories we feel nostalgia for are usually social. We rarely miss an empty room; we miss the people in it. Even the ambient sounds return: in my memory of that kitchen, I can hear the ambient hum of the refrigerator, the radio playing softly and my grandmother humming along.

Nostalgia can become a trap if we use it to hide from the present, to live in yesterday's world instead of today's. Used well, however, it works more like a bridge. When I bake that bread now, I think of it as a small homage to my grandmother, an homage paid not with words but with flour, water and patience. One day, perhaps, my children will bake a loaf of their own and remember a kitchen they have half forgotten. That, I think, is what nostalgia is for.

Questions:
How was nostalgia first understood?
It was described as a sickness that a Swiss medical student had seen in soldiers far from home.
Why did the grandmother's kitchen smell smoky?
The old wood stove leaked when the wind blew from the north.
What objects did the narrator find in the box?
She found a carving of a bird, a ticket from the exposition in Seattle and a pressed rose.
What happened when she touched a petal?
The petal broke into dust.
How does the narrator think of baking the bread now?
She thinks of it as a small homage to her grandmother.

lessons.title: The Commodore and the Cadet
lessons.summary: A retired naval officer and a teenage neighbor restore a small sailboat together and become friends.
lessons.text:
Walter Hale had retired from the navy with the rank of commodore, one step above captain, and at eighty-four he still stood as if he were on the deck of a ship. Since his hip operation, however, he walked with a limp, and the limp annoyed him. He drove an old gray sedan to the grocery store twice a week and spent the rest of his time in his garage, where a small wooden sailboat sat on two blocks, waiting to be repaired.

Marcus Diaz lived across the street. He was fifteen, he played midfield on his high school soccer team, and he had recently joined a youth program for future sailors, where he was a cadet. When he learned that the old man across the street had been a commodore, he could hardly believe it. One spring afternoon he knocked on the garage door and asked, a little shyly, whether a cadet could help a commodore with his boat.

Walter looked at him for a long moment and then handed him a piece of sandpaper.

The boat needed a great deal of work. The paint on the hull was cracked, the seats in the cockpit were soft with rot, and the mast had been bent in a storm years before. Walter explained that the cockpit is the open space where the sailors sit and steer, and he showed Marcus how to cut new boards for it. Marcus did the kneeling and the lifting; Walter did the measuring and the talking. He told stories about storms in the Pacific and about the first time he had climbed a mast at sea, when he was barely older than Marcus.

The hardest job was the mast. They could not afford a new one, so they decided to straighten the old one. It took three weekends. They warmed the wood, bent it slowly against a frame and left it to dry. Twice it sprang back. The third time, it stayed straight. When they stood the mast up in the garage, Walter put his hand on it and said nothing for a while.

In return, Marcus asked Walter to come to a soccer game. His team was undefeated that season. Walter parked the sedan near the field and sat in the front row of the stands. When Marcus scored from midfield in the last minute, the crowd started chanting the team's name, and Walter, to his own surprise, found himself chanting with them. The team stayed undefeated until the end of the season.

In August, the boat went into the water at last. Walter sat in the cockpit with the rope in his hands, and Marcus pushed them away from the dock. The wind filled the sail, and the straightened mast held. For an hour, nobody on the lake could have guessed which of them had a limp.

Questions:
Why did Walter walk with a limp?
He had had an operation on his hip.
What did Marcus do on his soccer team?
He played midfield.
What is the cockpit of a sailboat?
It is the open space where the sailors sit and steer.
How did Walter and Marcus straighten the mast?
They warmed the wood, bent it slowly against a frame and left it to dry.
What did Walter do when the crowd started chanting?
To his own surprise, he found himself chanting with them.

lessons.title: Living with Envy
lessons.summary: A columnist describes her envy of a cousin's glamorous life and what she learned about living with it.
lessons.text:
I should begin with a confession: I am an envious person. Not terribly, I hope, but often. For years the main object of my envy was my cousin Claire, who works for a multinational company and seems to spend half her life in airports. Her photos arrive from Tokyo, from Lisbon, from a beach whose name I cannot pronounce.

Envy is an uncomfortable emotion because it combines admiration and resentment. We admire what the other person has, and we resent them for having it. Philosophers have warned against it since ancient times. Yet it remains vastly common, and vastly underestimated as a force in our lives. Most of us simply do not talk about it, because admitting envy feels like admitting defeat.

What I have learned, slowly, is that envy is built on a portrayal rather than on a person. What I envied was not Claire herself but the portrayal of her life that reached me through a small screen: the views, the restaurants, the smiling colleagues. When we finally spent a weekend together last fall, I discovered the disparity between that portrayal and the facts. She was tired and missed her friends. She envied me, of all people, for living near my parents and for having a garden. The disparity was so large that I almost laughed.

Advertising feeds envy deliberately. Every season brings a fresh blitz of images showing people who are more beautiful, more relaxed and more successful than we are. The blitz works because it suggests that happiness comes from the accumulation of things: the right car, the right kitchen. But the accumulation of things rarely satisfies for long, and the people in the advertisements are paid to smile. The same is true of the entertainer whose life looks perfect on television; an entertainer is paid to make things look easy.

Envy also depends on a quiet belief that good things are scarce, as if life were a single pie and every slice someone else eats is a slice taken from us. Sometimes that is true; jobs and prizes can be scarce. More often it is not. My friend Nina opened a small clothing boutique last year, on the same street as another boutique that had been there for a decade. She expected the older shop to see her as a rival. Instead, its owner sent her customers and gave her advice, and both shops are doing well.

Magazines love lists of envy busters: count your blessings, take a walk. Some busters help. The best one I have found, however, is simpler. When I notice envy, I ask what it is telling me about my own wishes. Envying Claire told me I wanted to travel more. So this spring I took a trip to the mountains, three hours by train. It was wonderful, and I did not post a single photo.

Questions:
Why did the columnist envy her cousin Claire?
Claire works for a multinational company and sends photos from all over the world.
What disparity did the columnist discover?
She discovered a large disparity between the portrayal of Claire's life and the facts.
Why does the advertising blitz work?
It suggests that happiness comes from the accumulation of things.
What happened when Nina opened her boutique?
The owner of the older boutique sent her customers and gave her advice.
What is the best envy buster the columnist has found?
She asks what her envy is telling her about her own wishes.

lessons.title: The Quiet Language of a Long Marriage
lessons.summary: An old couple spends an ordinary morning together, saying very little and understanding everything.
lessons.text:
Harold and June Pruitt have been married for fifty-two years, and on most mornings they say fewer than a hundred words to each other before lunch. Visitors sometimes take this for a lack of warmth. It is the opposite. Over half a century, their conversation has been compressed, the way a long letter can be compressed into a single line by someone who knows the reader well.

The day begins in the kitchen, at a rectangular wooden table that Harold built the year they bought the house. It stands under the window, and from his end of the rectangular table Harold can see the bird feeder in the garden. He watches the sparrows perch on its edge, one after another, while June makes coffee. "Cardinal," he says, when a red bird arrives to perch among the gray ones. June looks up, nods and pours his cup. That is a complete conversation.

June is the tidy one. She cannot leave a cup in the sink or a newspaper on a chair, and she will tidy a room that is already tidy, simply because her hands like to be busy. Harold is not tidy at all, but he learned long ago to put his shoes by the door, and she learned not to mention his desk. Their friends say they have handled their differences wisely. Harold says they simply ran out of energy to argue.

After breakfast they cook together, because they always cook a proper lunch. Harold peels a carrot with slow, careful movements, then another carrot, and passes them across without being asked. June takes out the old electric mixer for a cake. The mixer is forty years old and louder than a truck, and when she turns it on, they cannot converse at all. It does not matter. Her hand on his shoulder means "move," and his raised eyebrow means "too much sugar." They converse the way musicians in a band do, through small signals that nobody else would notice.

Their children worry that this quiet is a sign of loneliness. Researchers who study long marriages suggest something different. Many happy older couples, they find, reach a kind of equilibrium, a balance in which neither partner needs constant comfort or praise. The equilibrium is not perfect, and it must be repaired after every argument, but it allows long silences to feel comfortable instead of threatening.

In the afternoon, Harold and June walk to the end of their street and back. She holds his arm loosely, not because she needs support, but because her hand has rested there for fifty years. Her fingers rest loosely on his sleeve, the way a scarf rests on a coat. They stop at the corner to look at the river, as they always do. Neither of them says anything, and both of them chose that silence wisely, a long time ago.

Questions:
Why do Harold and June say so little to each other?
Over fifty years, their conversation has been compressed.
What does Harold watch from the rectangular table?
He watches the sparrows perch on the edge of the bird feeder.
Why can't they converse while June uses the mixer?
The mixer is forty years old and louder than a truck.
What equilibrium do many happy older couples reach?
They reach a balance in which neither partner needs constant comfort or praise.
How does June hold Harold's arm on their walk?
She holds it loosely, because her hand has rested there for fifty years.

lessons.title: Homesick in Maine
lessons.summary: A young woman from an Austrian mountain village writes to her mother about homesickness in her first months in Maine.
lessons.text:
Dear Mama,

I have been in Maine for three months now, and I promised to write honestly. For the first six weeks, I was more homesick than I have ever been in my life.

Everything was unfamiliar. The food was unfamiliar, the jokes were unfamiliar, and even the light was unfamiliar, flatter and wider than the light in our valley. I missed our alpine village more than I expected. I missed the church bells, the sound of the cows on the high pasture and the way the mountains close around the village like a pair of hands. On my first walk, I followed a paved road for an hour and never saw a hill.

My surname caused problems from the first day. Nobody here can pronounce Steinwender. At the bank, the clerk called me "Miss Stein-something," and at the university my name was printed wrong on my student card. A small thing, I know, but far from home, even your own surname can feel like a coat that does not fit.

By October I was discouraged. My English was good enough for lectures but not for parties, where everyone talks at once. I sat in my room in the evenings and looked at photos of the pasture behind our house. I almost called you to say that I wanted to come home. I am glad I did not, because then things began to change.

Ruth, a woman from my economics class, invited me to her family's farm for a weekend. Her parents are potato growers, and her father is the third potato grower in his family. Their fields lie in the far north of the state, where the soil is dark and fertile; her father proudly called it the most fertile soil on the East Coast. When I described our alpine meadows, he listened as if I were describing another planet. For the first time, I felt that where I come from was interesting, not just far away.

On the drive back, we stopped because a moose was standing in the middle of the paved road. Mama, a moose is enormous, much bigger than a cow, with legs like a table. It looked at us without fear and walked slowly into the trees. Ruth said that seeing a moose brings good luck.

Last weekend we went to the coast, where the sand forms long, low hills. Ruth climbed to the top of a dune, and I followed her. From the top of the dune, you can see the ocean on one side and the forest on the other. It is nothing like home, and yet, standing there, I did not feel lost.

I still miss you, and the bells, and the mountains. But I am no longer discouraged.

With love,
Anna

Questions:
What did Anna miss about her alpine village?
She missed the church bells, the sound of the cows on the high pasture and the mountains around the village.
Why did her surname cause problems?
Nobody in Maine could pronounce Steinwender, and her name was printed wrong on her student card.
What do Ruth's parents grow?
They are potato growers, and their fields have dark, fertile soil.
Why did they stop on the drive back?
A moose was standing in the middle of the paved road.
What could Anna see from the top of the dune?
She could see the ocean on one side and the forest on the other.

lessons.title: Forgiveness, Weighed Calmly
lessons.summary: An essay on what forgiveness is and is not, told through two brothers and an unpaid loan.
lessons.text:
Forgiveness is often described as a single act, like signing a document. In practice it is closer to a process with several stages, and it has more than one facet. It helps to look at each facet separately, the way you might turn a stone in your hand to see each side.

Consider two brothers, Tom and Eli. Six years ago, Tom lent Eli five thousand dollars to start a small painting business. The business failed within a year, and the money was never returned. Eli, the borrower, was ashamed and stopped calling. Tom, the lender, was hurt and stopped calling too. For five years they saw each other only at family dinners, where they talked about the weather.

The first facet of forgiveness is emotional. It means letting go of resentment, the bitter feeling that returns every time we remember the injury. Many traditions describe this as a kind of washing. People speak of the need to cleanse the heart, as if anger were dirt that builds up over time. Psychologists agree that resentment tends to harm the person who carries it. Some writers use the image of a river: what we hold onto at the source flows downstream into everything else, into our sleep, our work and our other relationships. A quarrel between two brothers flows downstream to their children, who grow up hardly knowing their cousins.

The second facet is practical, and it is often confused with the first. Forgiving someone does not necessarily mean forgetting what happened or pretending it did not matter. Tom could forgive Eli and still decide never to lend him money again. He could forgive the borrower and still expect an apology. Philosophers do not agree unanimously on many things, but most of them agree that forgiveness and trust are separate. Trust has to be rebuilt; forgiveness can be given.

After a long quarrel, we tend to perform an autopsy on it, going over every detail in search of the cause. The autopsy can be useful for a while, because it helps us understand what went wrong. But an autopsy that never ends keeps the wound open. At some point, the useful question is no longer "Who was to blame?" but "What do we want now?"

Last spring, at their mother's birthday party, the family voted unanimously that the two brothers should sit together. Somewhere between the soup and the cake, Eli said that he was sorry about the money and that he had been too ashamed to say so. Tom said that he had missed his brother more than the money. It did not cleanse every bitter memory at once, and Eli is still paying the money back, a little each month. But the two families now spend weekends together, and the cousins have finally become friends.

Questions:
What are the two facets of forgiveness described in the essay?
One facet is emotional, letting go of resentment, and the other is practical.
Why did the borrower stop calling his brother?
Eli was ashamed because his business had failed and he had not returned the money.
How does resentment flow downstream?
It flows into our sleep, our work and our other relationships, and even to our children.
When is the autopsy of a quarrel useful?
It is useful for a while, because it helps us understand what went wrong.
What did the family decide unanimously?
They voted unanimously that the two brothers should sit together.

lessons.title: The Occupant of 4B
lessons.summary: A young musician and the elderly man in the apartment above her turn a complaint about noise into a friendship.
lessons.text:
Priya had lived in apartment 3B for only a week when she found the note under her door. It was written in careful, old-fashioned letters. "Dear new neighbor," it said, "your music is very good, but it arrives in my kitchen through the ventilation. Could we discuss this? Gus, the occupant of 4B."

Priya was a guitarist, and she practiced every evening with a small amplifier. She had not realized that the old building's ventilation carried sound so well. She felt embarrassed. That evening she climbed the stairs, knocked on the door of 4B and met its occupant: a thin man of about eighty with a white beard and reading glasses pushed up on his forehead.

Gus invited her in, and she understood the problem immediately. There was an air vent above his stove that led straight down to her apartment, and through it Gus could hear her guitar as clearly as a radio. He was not angry. He said that he liked the guitar, but not at eleven o'clock at night, and not quite so loud.

They agreed on a plan. Priya would turn the amplifier down and stop playing at nine. She also bought foam panels to insulate the wall near her desk, and she asked the building manager whether he could insulate the ventilation too. The manager laughed and said the building was a hundred years old; nobody could insulate it completely. The panels helped anyway.

Gus, it turned out, was a retired chemistry teacher who could not eat gluten, a protein found in wheat that made him ill. He missed bread more than anything. Priya's mother had a recipe for a flat bread made without gluten, and the following Sunday Priya brought him a warm stack of it. He ate three pieces standing in the kitchen.

After that, they helped each other in small ways. In July, a wasp built a nest on Gus's balcony, and he was afraid to step outside. Priya, who had grown up on a farm, waited until evening, when the wasps were calm, and removed the nest with a plastic bag. Only one wasp followed her, and it did not sting. In return, Gus taught her to reuse the glass jars that she had been throwing away. He would reuse everything if he could: jars, bags, string, even envelopes.

The building's courtyard had its own small dramas. Two cats, one orange and one black, met there almost every night, and their brawl woke half the building. Gus said that the brawl had been going on for three years and that neither cat had ever won. Priya wrote a short, funny song about it and played it for him, quietly, before nine.

By the end of the year, the note from Gus was framed on Priya's wall. Under it, she had written a single line: "The best complaint I ever received."

Questions:
How did Priya's music reach Gus's kitchen?
It arrived through the building's ventilation.
What did Priya do to insulate her apartment?
She bought foam panels to insulate the wall near her desk.
Why could Gus not eat ordinary bread?
He could not eat gluten, a protein found in wheat that made him ill.
How did Priya remove the wasp nest?
She waited until evening, when the wasps were calm, and removed the nest with a plastic bag.
What did Gus teach Priya?
He taught her to reuse glass jars instead of throwing them away.

lessons.title: The Hot Springs
lessons.summary: A busy engineer takes his elderly father on a slow trip to the hot springs of Yellowstone.
lessons.text:
Daniel had been promising his father a trip for years. He worked as an engineer at a semiconductor plant in Arizona, where he helped design the tiny chips inside phones and cars, and there was always another deadline. When his father, Martin, turned seventy-eight, Daniel finally took two weeks off, and they drove north to Yellowstone, the national park famous for its hot springs.

Martin had a heart condition, and before they left, his doctor reminded them both about his medicine. He carried small sublingual tablets in his shirt pocket. A sublingual tablet is placed under the tongue, where it dissolves quickly and enters the blood. "If you feel pain in your chest," the doctor said, "take one sublingual tablet, sit down and wait." Daniel checked his father's pocket every morning, and Martin pretended to be annoyed.

The first thing they noticed in the park was the smell. The air around the hot springs smells of sulfur, like old eggs, because the water carries sulfur up from deep underground. Then they saw the springs themselves: pools of blue, green and orange, with white vapor rising from them into the cold morning air. The vapor drifted across the wooden paths, so that the other visitors appeared and disappeared like figures in a dream.

They did not hurry. Daniel had planned to ascend a trail to a high viewpoint on the second day, but Martin tired quickly on the hills. So they chose a shorter path and took an hour to ascend it, stopping on every bench. At the top, they sat and waited for a famous hot spring that throws water into the air every hour or so. When it finally did, the water shot violently into the sky, higher than a house, and fell back as rain and vapor. The ground seemed to shake violently for a moment, although Martin insisted that it was only his knees.

On the benches, they talked more than they had in years. Martin had taught history for forty years, and he told Daniel about the Cold War, when the world was divided between two great powers. Historians call it a bipolar world, he explained, a world with two poles, like a magnet. In a bipolar world, he said, every small country had to choose a side. Daniel, in turn, tried to explain what a semiconductor is: a material that sometimes lets electricity pass and sometimes stops it, which is what makes computers possible. Martin understood perhaps half of it, but he asked good questions.

On the last evening, they sat outside their cabin and watched the vapor rise from a distant valley, pink in the sunset. Martin had not needed a single tablet. "We should have done this ten years ago," he said. Daniel agreed. Then he said that they would do it again next year, and this time he meant it.

Questions:
Where did Daniel work?
He worked as an engineer at a semiconductor plant in Arizona.
How does a sublingual tablet work?
It is placed under the tongue, where it dissolves quickly and enters the blood.
Why does the air around the hot springs smell of sulfur?
The water carries sulfur up from deep underground.
How long did it take them to ascend the shorter path?
It took them an hour, because they stopped on every bench.
What is a bipolar world, according to Martin?
It is a world divided between two great powers, with two poles like a magnet.
